name: Acetazolamide (Diamox)
lead: Acetazolamide, sold under the brand name Diamox among others, is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases the kidney's excretion of bicarbonate, sodium and water, which makes it a mild diuretic. It is an older prescription drug used for glaucoma, certain edemas, some seizure disorders and the prevention of acute mountain sickness.[1][2][9]

In appearance-focused communities it is mentioned in the context of "depuffing", because a diuretic reduces body fluid and people who want a leaner, less swollen look sometimes ask about diuretics in general. The chain proponents describe is: more water excreted, less fluid held in the tissues, a drier-looking face or physique. No published study has tested acetazolamide for facial puffiness, facial water retention or any cosmetic outcome.[1] On bodybuilding forums it appears mostly in two contexts: as a drug taken by climbers for altitude sickness, and as a diuretic whose detection in drug tests is asked about before contests.[11][12][13]

Its studied uses are medical. A randomized trial in acute decompensated heart failure examined it as an add-on to loop diuretics, and a trial in idiopathic intracranial hypertension examined it for protecting vision.[3][4] Labelled adverse effects include metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, tingling sensations and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions.[2] Wikipedia lists acetazolamide among substances prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[9]

paras: Appearance-related interest centers on its diuretic action. Because carbonic anhydrase inhibition reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water in the kidney's proximal tubule, urine output rises.[1][9] Some people in appearance and physique communities therefore list it with other diuretics when talking about reducing puffiness or water weight. No trial has measured facial puffiness, facial water retention or any other cosmetic outcome with acetazolamide.[1]

In physique sport forums, a 2007 T Nation thread titled around contest advice includes a question about how long acetazolamide can be detected, which reflects the drug's place on anti-doping lists; other T Nation members mention it as a drug they carry for high-altitude climbs.[11][12][13]

The US label lists adjunctive treatment of edema due to congestive heart failure and drug-induced edema, centrencephalic epilepsies, chronic open-angle and secondary glaucoma, and preoperative lowering of eye pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma. It is also labelled for preventing or easing symptoms of acute mountain sickness in climbers making rapid ascents.[2]

Wikipedia describes use in menstrual-related seizures and as an add-on in refractory epilepsy, as well as off-label use for central sleep apnea, hemiplegic migraine prevention, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, Meniere's disease and kidney protection during high-dose methotrexate.[9] Reference works also list periodic paralysis and metabolic alkalosis in critical care.[1] Reviews of periodic paralysis and familial hemiplegic migraine discuss it among the treatments.[14][15]

Carbonic anhydrase is a zinc-containing enzyme that catalyses the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and a proton.[7] Acetazolamide inhibits it, which in the proximal tubule reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water, producing a mild diuresis and a metabolic acidosis.[1] The same inhibition reduces aqueous humor formation in the eye.[1] Wikipedia adds that the resulting acidification of the blood stimulates faster breathing and raises blood oxygen, which underlies its use for altitude acclimatization.[9]
Wikipedia gives protein binding of 70 to 90 percent, no metabolism, an elimination half-life of 2 to 4 hours and about 90 percent excretion unchanged in urine.[9]

The label lists headache, fatigue, gastrointestinal upset, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalance including low potassium and sodium, and rare blood disorders and liver injury.[2] Wikipedia also lists tingling in the extremities, drowsiness, taste changes, reduced libido, polyuria and kidney stones.[9]

The label carries a warning that fatalities have occurred, rarely, from severe sulfonamide-type reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, and that sensitization can recur on re-exposure.[2] Contraindications described include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, impaired kidney function, marked liver disease and states of low sodium, low potassium or hyperchloremic acidosis.[9]
Animal studies have shown limb defects with acetazolamide, and there are no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women, according to the label.[2]
No studies found on acetazolamide for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing; the research covers its medical indications.

In the ADVOR randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2022, intravenous acetazolamide was tested as an add-on to loop diuretics in patients hospitalised with acute decompensated heart failure and volume overload, with successful decongestion within three days as the primary end point.[3] A Swiss review of the trial describes significantly faster decongestion on a clinical score with few side effects.[18] A later registered phase 4 trial examined oral acetazolamide for decompensated heart failure in 400 participants.[10]

The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial (JAMA, 2014) evaluated acetazolamide on visual function in people with mild visual loss.[4] An observational study of 278 hikers in Nepal in 1976 examined the incidence of acute mountain sickness and its prophylaxis, and a later Lancet review covers high-altitude illness.[5][6] A phase 4 trial has examined dosing for obstructive sleep apnea.[8]

Wikipedia dates the compound to a 1951 US patent by chemists J. W. Clapp Jr. and R. O. Roblin assigned to American Cyanamid, with medical use from 1952; Grokipedia attributes the synthesis to Roblin and Clapp at Lederle Laboratories, with pharmacology by Thomas H. Maren, and gives a 1953 US approval.[1][9] A 1955 Minnesota Medicine article titled "Diamox" and a 1963 Canadian Medical Association Journal article on epilepsy treatment show its early clinical adoption.[16][17] It is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and is available as a generic.[9]

Acetazolamide is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, where it is Schedule 4.[9] It appears in Wikipedia's list of WADA prohibited substances, as a diuretic and masking agent category.[9]
Public discussion of acetazolamide in lifting and physique communities is sparse and mostly concerns altitude medicine and drug-test questions, rather than facial depuffing protocols.[12][13]

card.summary: A sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness; it is a diuretic, but nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.
card.note: Prescription drug with rare serious sulfonamide-type reactions; no appearance studies.

quick.overview:
Acetazolamide (Diamox) is an older prescription diuretic that blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Doctors use it for glaucoma, some forms of edema, certain seizure disorders, raised pressure inside the skull and the prevention of altitude sickness.

It is grouped under depuffing because it makes the body shed fluid, but no study has tested it for facial puffiness or any cosmetic goal.
quick.mechanism: By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, it reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water in the kidney and lowers fluid production in the eye, causing mild diuresis and a metabolic acidosis.
quick.risks: The label lists tingling, fatigue, stomach upset, acid-base and electrolyte disturbances, and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions and blood disorders. It is prescription-only in the US and carries a pregnancy caution based on animal limb defects.
